430	  Rigorous verdict coexist with a section of malformed chains.
431	
432	- **Hand-wavy** — some conclusions lack derivation chains; OR chains reference GT-IDs that
433	  do not appear in the Ground Truths section; OR an analogy is used as direct evidence
434	  ("others have solved it this way," "industry standard is X") without grounding in a named
435	  GT about that other situation; OR the Abandoned Reasoning section uses the honest-depth
436	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
437	  "no dead ends were encountered," "all reasoning paths worked"); OR a hop the endpoint
438	  depends on does not follow by deduction or cited regularity (a non-sequitur) — including
439	  a hop whose only gap is an undeclared premise — or an arithmetic error changes the endpoint; an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged
440	  is the Sound clause above, not this one — **this clause is why the criterion cannot be scored
441	  on form alone either.** A chain can name
442	  its inputs, carry a genuine intermediate, render every hop in the prescribed form and reach
443	  a conclusion while a hop the endpoint depends on does not follow.
444	
445	- **Absent** — no derivation chains exist in the document; OR the Derivation Chains section
446	  is absent or empty; OR conclusions appear in section 6 with no corresponding chains in
447	  section 4 — the core question's answer cannot be traced to any named ground truth.
448	
449	### Criterion 5: Validate
450	
451	Scores the **signed-off analysis** — the complete output with all conclusions traced and weak
452	links resolved or explicitly flagged with confidence caveats — across all six output sections,
453	focusing on the confidence caveats attached to the Derivation Chains (output section 4).
454	
455	- **Rigorous** — every derivation chain's weakest link is named; every MEDIUM or LOW confidence
456	  caveat, on a chain or on the Conclusion section, explains only its own rating: it names each
457	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, with the verification that would remove that input as a
458	  cause of the downgrade, and each Cn its head cites — or, for the Conclusion section, each
459	  contributing chain — that is rated below HIGH, and it need not re-explain a named Cn, whose
460	  own caveat carries its explanation; and for each downgrade cause belonging to the chain or
461	  Conclusion itself, such as a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation, it states
462	  what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path
463	  exists, that reason being either, for an absent-fails derivation, the absent-fails EXCEPT
464	  clause below, the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, or an explicit
465	  account of why no available evidence settles that cause;
466	  the overall Conclusion section's confidence rating (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW) matches the weakest
467	  chain that contributes to it, counting only chains not covered by an EXCEPT clause stated in
468	  this same descriptor; no chain that consumes a GT-N? input is rated HIGH confidence; every
469	  chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites, a ceiling that holds
470	  even when a cited chain is rated MEDIUM under an EXCEPT clause below.
471	  Every rating is calibrated: each chain carries the band its inputs, hops and rivals
472	  license under the three-axis definition in `output-template.md` — no chain rated above
473	  what those axes permit, and none rated below it. A Conclusion claim supported by
474	  at least one HIGH-confidence chain may be presented at HIGH; a claim with no such
475	  chain is presented at the band its weakest contributing chain licenses, and presenting
476	  it so is Rigorous rather than a shortfall. Under-rating is a defect of the same kind
477	  as over-rating, and this criterion scores calibration, not altitude. EXCEPT: a chain is explicitly marked speculative — for
478	  example `[Speculative]` — and the analysis states, in the same place, that the claim it
479	  supports is not load-bearing and is offered for exploration only; that mark plus that
480	  statement is the satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM, though its confidence
481	  line still gives each of its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account
482	  of why no available evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason; a
483	  speculative chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer satisfies this
484	  EXCEPT clause, so a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another
485	  chain's head and instead stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (output section 5).
486	  EXCEPT: a chain is
487	  an absent-fails derivation — of the form "if [assumption] were true we could conclude X;
488	  [assumption] is false; therefore X does not follow" — whose named false assumption is the
489	  satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM because it establishes what does not
490	  follow rather than what does.
491	
492	  The adversarial pass Phase 5 prescribes has run and its record is complete: each computed
493	  figure's recompute, the sensitivity ground truth and whether it is `?`-marked, the rival and
494	  where it is ruled out or carried live, a premise stated in the past tense, an unfiltered
495	  cause list written before any grouping, clusters each naming the chain ids or ground-truth
496	  ids the weakness bears on, per cluster a named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk
497	  with a named mitigation, and the falsification condition — each part present or carrying its
498	  step's not-applicable line. Each structural weakness the pass
499	  returned has landed somewhere a reader can find it — as a named weak link on a chain, or as
500	  an explicit confidence caveat on the conclusion it threatens. An analysis whose conclusion is
501	  neither a plan nor a claim satisfies the Premise, Causes, Clusters and Disposition parts by
502	  carrying the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line with its reason named — that
503	  line is the adversarial-technique step's own not-applicable line, not a waiver of the whole
504	  record, so the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts each still carry their
505	  content or their own step's not-applicable line; an analysis that does carry a plan or a claim
506	  cannot satisfy the technique step that way, and the reason given is what makes the two cases
507	  distinguishable.
508	
509	  **A conclusion without a HIGH chain is not a shortfall.** A conclusion resting on no
510	  HIGH-confidence chain, uncovered by either EXCEPT clause above, is Rigorous on this
511	  criterion when every band it rests on is the band that chain's axes license and the
512	  Conclusion's own rating equals its weakest contributing chain's. A MEDIUM or LOW overall
513	  Conclusion rating remains a legitimate, honestly-caveated analysis — `output-template.md`
514	  permits it and this criterion now scores it Rigorous when it is calibrated. What bands
515	  this criterion below Rigorous is a band that does not match its axes in either direction,
516	  never a band that is merely low, and a verdict block reporting Rigorous alongside a
517	  MEDIUM overall rating is the expected shape of an honest analysis rather than a
518	  contradiction. An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one of the
519	  two EXCEPT clauses above names it in the Criterion 5 verdict block and cites the evidence
520	  that clause requires; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the analysis's behalf.
521	
522	- **Sound** — confidence ratings exist on chains, but a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line omits a
523	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, or a Cn its head cites (or, on the Conclusion section, a
524	  contributing chain) that is rated below HIGH, or a downgrade cause belonging to its own chain
525	  or Conclusion — including a MEDIUM or LOW rating that no named GT-N? input or Cn accounts for
526	  and whose line names no cause of its own; OR a confidence line names a GT-N? input without the
527	  verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; OR a confidence line gives a
528	  downgrade cause belonging to its own chain or Conclusion with neither what would remove it as
529	  a cause of the downgrade nor a permitted no-path reason — for an absent-fails derivation, the
530	  absent-fails EXCEPT clause, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that
531	  cause — including a line whose only account of such a cause is the speculative EXCEPT clause
532	  or any clause other than the absent-fails one; OR a chain's head cites a chain marked
533	  speculative that has no verification path; OR a chain is rated HIGH confidence while consuming
534	  a GT-N? input (the rating does not match the unverified-input rule); OR a chain is rated above
535	  the lowest-rated chain its head cites; OR a single chain's band does not match what its
536	  three axes license, in either direction — a chain rated HIGH whose head carries a `?` or
537	  whose hops rest on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise, or a chain meeting all three axes
538	  rated MEDIUM — while every other chain in the analysis is correctly banded; OR an
539	  adversarial pass record, or the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line, is present
540	  but one or more of the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts is absent and
541	  carries no not-applicable line of its own — a step silently omitted from a pass that otherwise
542	  ran.
543	
544	- **Hand-wavy** — confidence ratings appear on the overall Conclusion section but are absent
545	  from individual derivation chains; OR weak links are described in general terms ("some
546	  assumptions remain uncertain") without naming the specific chain step or GT-N? input that
547	  caused the concern; OR an adversarial pass record is present but no cluster carries a
548	  disposition — neither a named plan change nor an explicitly accepted risk with a named
549	  mitigation — so the pass named structural weaknesses and acted on none of them; OR the record
550	  states its clusters without the cause list they were drawn from, which is the generic risk
551	  list the pass exists to replace rather than a pass that produced one; OR two or more
552	  chains carry bands their axes do not license, so the miscalibration is a pattern rather
553	  than an isolated entry; OR every chain in the analysis carries the same band and no
554	  confidence line names which axis produced it, which is a default setting rather than a
555	  rating.
556	
557	- **Absent** — no confidence ratings appear anywhere in the derivation chains; OR GT-N? inputs
558	  are used in load-bearing chains without any confidence caveat anywhere in the document; OR
559	  — covering the case the first two clauses miss — confidence ratings exist but no weak-link
560	  identification or chain inspection was performed at all, so there is no evidence that
561	  Phase 5's stress-test operation was executed; OR neither an adversarial pass record nor an
562	  `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line appears anywhere in the response, so there
563	  is no evidence that Phase 5's adversarial pass was executed at all. These two clauses are
564	  separate readings: a weakest-link paragraph written by the same reasoning that built the
565	  chains satisfies the first and not the second, and an analysis scoring above Absent on the
566	  strength of that paragraph alone is what this clause exists to catch.
567	
568	### Criterion 6: Conclusion-to-Ground-Truth Traceability
569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. Quoted span: where the band is determined by whether a section-6 claim traces to a named section-4 chain, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's claim-inventory table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Conclusion prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Key Insight being a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a non-obvious finding — a semantic property the claim-inventory table carries no column for — quote the analysis text directly.
573	
574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
597	
598	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
599	
600	---
601	
602	## Usage Note
603	
604	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
605	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
606	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
607	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
608	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
609	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
610	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring
611	again. This closing note restates that bound; it does not create a second, looser one.

3	# Pre-Mortem
4	
5	> A prospective-hindsight failure analysis tool. Reach for this when a proposed
6	> plan needs stress-testing before commitment — the goal is to surface probable
7	> failure causes before they materialise.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to reach for this
12	
13	Use a pre-mortem once a plan has enough specificity to reason about particular
14	failure modes, but before it is finalised and carries organizational momentum.
15	Not the right tool for evaluating options (use trade-off analysis) or for tracing
16	something that already went wrong (use 5-Whys).
17	
18	**Decision rule — pre-mortem vs. inversion:** pre-mortem stress-tests a **plan**;
19	[inversion](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/agents/references/inversion.md) stress-tests a **claim**. If a concrete plan with actions and a
20	timeline exists, pre-mortem is the right tool — it reasons about implementation failure
21	modes that claim-level inversion cannot see. With only a stated belief, conclusion, or
22	design principle in hand, inversion fits better. This is the same boundary
23	`inversion.md` states from its own side, and it is the one that matters most here:
24	Phase 5 selects between these two directly, so a reader arriving from that
25	prescription needs to know why they were sent here rather than there.
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Framing
30	
31	Before any other step, adopt this premise explicitly:
32	
33	> It is approximately six months from now. This plan has failed — not merely
34	> underperformed, but failed badly. That outcome is a fact.
35	> Working backward: what caused it?
36	
37	This past-tense framing is not rhetorical. It bypasses the optimism bias that
38	makes forward-looking risk lists generic. Do not skip it or soften it to
39	"might fail" — the grammatical shift from possibility to accomplished fact is
40	the mechanism.
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Procedure
45	
46	1. **Restate the premise.** Before writing anything, say or write: "The plan has
47	   already failed. What caused it?" This re-anchors the prospective-hindsight
48	   frame before analysis begins.
49	
50	2. **Write independently.** List every cause of the failure without filtering —
51	   write the full list before reviewing it. Do not discard causes that seem
52	   unlikely; the list is raw material, not a verdict. Generate from at least
53	   three named viewpoints — for example the implementer, the person who has to
54	   live with the result, whoever pays for it, and a competitor who benefits
55	   from the failure. One generator asked once returns one perspective's
56	   failures, and the causes it misses are systematically the ones outside the
57	   frame it was asked in.
58	
59	3. **Interrogate the list adversarially.** Re-read each item and ask which ones
60	   contradict the plan's own stated premise, or the recommendation the analysis
61	   is about to make. A cause that would embarrass the conclusion is higher
62	   signal than one that merely adds risk to it. In a facilitated session these
63	   are the items a junior participant suppresses; written by a single analyst
64	   they are the items that get hedged into vagueness rather than dropped, so
65	   look for the softened ones, not the missing ones.
66	
67	4. **Identify recurring patterns.** Look for failure causes that cluster — the
68	   same root (over-optimistic timeline, single point of dependency, assumption
69	   never validated). A cluster is a structural weakness in the plan, not an
70	   isolated risk.
71	
72	5. **Triage each cluster on two axes: plausibility and recoverability.** Not by
73	   a probability figure invented for the purpose — say which of these it is:
74	
75	   - **Fatal** — if it happens, the plan does not recover. These get a plan
76	     change, not a mitigation, however unlikely they seem.
77	   - **Costly but survivable** — the plan continues at a stated price. These get
78	     a mitigation and an owner.
79	   - **Tolerable** — record and move on.
80	
81	   Sort by recoverability *before* plausibility. A fatal-but-unlikely cause
82	   outranks a likely-but-tolerable one, and ranking by likelihood alone inverts
83	   exactly that comparison — which is the failure a pre-mortem exists to catch.
84	
85	6. **Give every fatal and costly cluster a tripwire.** A tripwire is the
86	   **observation that would tell you this failure is now underway**, named in
87	   advance: a threshold, a date, a signal, a metric crossing a line. "Watch
88	   integration risk" is not a tripwire; "the staging sync job fails twice in one
89	   week" is, and "we have not got a test environment by 14 March" is.
90	
91	   State who would see it and when they would look. A failure mode nobody is
92	   positioned to notice has no tripwire, and saying so plainly is more useful
93	   than writing one that will never fire. The pre-mortem's value is spent at the
94	   moment the list is written unless something converts a predicted failure into
95	   a detected one — that is what the tripwire is.
96	
97	7. **Act on findings.** Modify the plan to address the structural weaknesses, or
98	   explicitly accept the risk with a named mitigation. A pre-mortem with no
99	   downstream plan change was box-ticking.
100	
101	**Exit criterion:** The failure has been stated as having already happened, causes
102	are written from that stance, causes are clustered into structural weaknesses,
103	every cluster carries a triage verdict of fatal / costly but survivable /
104	tolerable, every fatal and costly cluster carries a tripwire with an owner or an
105	explicit statement that no observable one exists, and every cluster has either a
106	named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk with a named mitigation. A
107	pre-mortem that ends without one of those two outcomes per cluster is
108	box-ticking, not a finding.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## Output contract
113	
114	The exit criterion above names four things the pre-mortem must produce. This is
115	what they look like on the page, in this order:
116	
117	**Premise** — one line, past tense, stating the failure as accomplished fact.
118	Not "the plan might fail"; the grammatical shift is the mechanism, and a premise
119	written in the conditional has already lost it.
120	
121	**Causes** — the unfiltered list, one per line, written before any grouping
122	appears. The viewpoints from step 2 are visible in it: if every cause is a
123	technical one, step 2 was run once rather than three times. Writing the clusters
124	first and back-filling causes into them inverts the procedure and produces the
125	generic risk list the whole framing exists to avoid.
126	
127	**Clusters** — the structural weaknesses the causes fall into, each named, and
128	each naming the causes it absorbs. A cluster is a claim that several causes share
129	one root; a heading with one cause under it is a cause, not a cluster. When the
130	pre-mortem runs inside a first-principles analysis, each cluster also cites the
131	chain ids (`Cn`) or ground-truth ids (`GT-N`) it bears on, so the finding lands
132	somewhere a reader can check it against.
133	
134	**Disposition** — per cluster, one of exactly two things: a named plan change, or
135	an explicitly accepted risk with a named mitigation. "Worth watching", "we should
136	keep this in mind" and "a risk we accept" with nothing named after it are none of
137	the above. A cluster whose disposition is an accepted risk still names what makes
138	the risk survivable; that is what distinguishes accepting a risk from noticing one.
139	
140	A pre-mortem missing any of the four has not run. A pre-mortem whose causes list
141	is shorter than its cluster list ran backwards.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Example
146	
147	**Plan:** Host a dinner party for twelve people in two weeks, cooking a full
148	three-course meal from scratch for the first time at this scale.
149	
150	**Framing applied:** It is two weeks from now. The dinner party has failed badly.
151	What caused it?
152	
153	**Backward-derived failure causes:**
154	- Underestimated preparation time; last two courses were served an hour late
155	- A key ingredient unavailable the day before; no substitution plan
156	- One course required equipment not owned and not sourced in advance
157	- Two guests had dietary restrictions not asked about until the day of
158	- Energy depleted by the time guests arrived; host unable to enjoy the evening
159	
160	**Pattern identified:** Every cause traces back to a single structural weakness —
161	no dry run at smaller scale and no contingency check before commitment. The plan
162	assumed novelty would resolve itself on the day.
163	
164	---
165	
166	## Failure modes
167	
168	**Forward-looking framing.** "What could go wrong?" produces a generic risk list.
169	If causes feel speculative and mild, the past-tense premise was not adopted.
170	
171	**Running it too early.** A pre-mortem on a plan with insufficient specificity
172	yields generic concerns. The plan must have enough detail to reason about
173	particular failure modes — vague plans produce vague analyses.
174	
175	**Anchoring (in group settings).** When facilitated, the most senior voice in the
176	room shapes the list. Run independent writing before any sharing — each
177	participant writes silently before the group compares lists.
178	
179	**First-speaker anchoring.** The first cause named draws subsequent thinking
180	toward it. Write exhaustively before ranking or grouping.
181	
182	**No follow-through.** A pre-mortem with no downstream plan change was
183	box-ticking. Findings must modify the plan or be explicitly accepted with
184	named mitigations.
185	
186	---
187	
188	## Handoff
189	
190	The probable failure causes identified here feed Phase 5 (Validate). Add the
191	highest-signal structural weaknesses to the adversarial validation pass — each
192	one is a weak-link candidate for the signed-off analysis to address or explicitly
193	accept.

3	# Trade-Off Analysis
4	
5	> Structures a choice between two or more genuinely viable options by weighting
6	> criteria before scoring — preventing the reverse-engineering of weights to
7	> justify a decision already made intuitively.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to reach for this
12	
13	Use this tool when two or more options are viable (none obviously dominant), the
14	choice spans multiple criteria that pull in different directions, and an
15	intuitive pick would be hard to justify to others.
16	
17	Do not use it when one option dominates on every relevant criterion — that is a
18	direct decision, not a trade-off.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Procedure
23	
24	1. **Name the options — including the status quo.** List each option being
25	   compared, and **always include doing nothing** as one of them, named as what
26	   it concretely is ("keep the current 70/30 split", "stay on REST/JSON"). A
27	   comparison whose option set is all-change silently assumes change is
28	   warranted and reports that assumption back as a finding. If the status quo is
29	   genuinely unavailable — a contract expires, the hardware is failing — say so
30	   in one line and list it as ruled out; do not omit it silently.
31	
32	2. **State the must-haves and apply them as knock-outs.** Before any scoring,
33	   name the conditions an option must satisfy to be viable at all. An option
34	   that fails a must-have is **eliminated, not scored low** — report it under
35	   `## Options` as knocked out, with the must-have it failed. Scoring a
36	   non-viable option lets a high weighted total out-vote a hard constraint,
37	   which is how an option that cannot actually be chosen wins a trade-off.
38	   If nothing is a must-have, write "no must-haves" rather than skipping the
39	   step — the two are different claims.
40	
41	3. **List criteria.** Identify 5–8 criteria that matter to this decision. Lock
42	   this list — add no new criteria after this step. If a criterion matters, it
43	   must appear now.
44	
45	4. **Assign weights. Lock them now.** Give each criterion a relative weight
46	   (1–5) before scoring any option. If you cannot assign weights without first
47	   seeing how options score, stop — locking weights before scoring is the core
48	   discipline that prevents reverse-engineering them to favor an intuitive pick.
49	
50	5. **Anchor the scale, then score.** Before scoring, state for each criterion
51	   what a **1** and a **5** concretely mean — the anchors. "Cost: 1 = over
52	   $20k, 5 = under $2k" is an anchor; "Cost: 1 = bad, 5 = good" is not. Then
53	   score each option on each criterion independently (1–5) against those
54	   anchors. Phrase every criterion so higher is always better (e.g.,
55	   "Reliability" not "Reliability risk") — a mixed scale silently inverts the
56	   result. Without anchors a score means only "how I felt about this option",
57	   and the arithmetic that follows inherits that and dresses it as a number.
58	
59	6. **Cite the ground truth each score rests on.** Every score names the
60	   `GT-ID`s that justify it. A score resting on a `GT-N?` input carries that
61	   `?` forward: per D-07, the chain this trade-off collapses into is capped at
62	   **MEDIUM** and its confidence line names the unverified input and the
63	   verification that would remove it. A score with no ground truth behind it is
64	   a preference — mark it as one rather than citing nothing.
65	
66	7. **Compute:** multiply weight × score per criterion; sum per option.
67	
68	8. **Read the result.** The highest weighted total among the surviving options
69	   is the recommendation. If it surprises you, only re-examine a weight when you
70	   can state why it was wrong *before* seeing the result — adjusting weights
71	   afterward is the failure mode this procedure prevents.
72	
73	**Flip test — run it every time, not only on a near-tie.** Report the
74	**smallest weight change that changes the winner**: name the criterion, the
75	weight it would have to move to, and how far that is from the weight you
76	locked. Then ask whether that weight is genuinely wrong. A winner that survives
77	only a ±1 move on one criterion is a near-tie whatever the totals look like,
78	and a winner that survives every single-criterion move is a robust result —
79	both are findings, and neither is visible from the totals alone. Report the
80	flip distance under `## Recommendation`. Do not refine scores to break a
81	near-tie; refining manufactures false precision. If no single-criterion change
82	flips the result, say that explicitly — "no single weight change flips this"
83	is the strongest result this procedure can return, and it is worth stating.
84	
85	---
86	
87	## Example
88	
89	**Decision:** Laptop for a parent who browses, video-calls, and writes
90	documents.
91	
92	**Ground truths this rests on:**
93	
94	- **GT-1** — the current machine drops video calls roughly weekly (observed over
95	  two months).
96	- **GT-2** — refurbished units from this vendor carry a 90-day warranty; new
97	  units carry 12 months (vendor's published terms, read at source).
98	- **GT-3?** — refurbished failure rates are "around twice" new in the first
99	  year. *Unverified — recalled from a review article, source not located.*
100	
101	**Step 1 — options named, status quo included:**
102	
103	- **A** — refurbished mid-range
104	- **B** — new entry-level
105	- **C** — keep the current laptop (status quo)
106	
107	**Step 2 — must-haves applied as knock-outs:**
108	
109	| Must-have | A | B | C |
110	|---|---|---|---|
111	| Holds a video call without dropping | ✓ | ✓ | **✗ (GT-1)** |
112	
113	**C is knocked out, not scored.** Had it been scored instead, its perfect cost
114	score (5 × 3 = 15, nothing to spend) would have carried it close to A on a
115	total — while still failing the one thing the machine is being replaced *for*.
116	This is the failure mode step 2 exists to prevent.
117	
118	**Steps 3-4 — criteria and weights locked before any scoring:**
119	
120	| Criterion                       | Weight | 1 means…                    | 5 means…                     |
121	|----------------------------------|--------|-----------------------------|------------------------------|
122	| Performance                      | 4      | stutters on a video call    | headroom for years           |
123	| Reliability                      | 5      | failure expected in year 1  | failure unlikely in 5 years  |
124	| Cost                             | 3      | over $900                   | under $300                   |
125	| Warranty / support               | 4      | none                        | 12 months or more            |
126	| Portability                      | 2      | desk-bound                  | carried daily without thought|
127	| Ease of setup (non-technical)    | 3      | needs a technical helper    | works out of the box         |
128	
129	**Step 5-7 — scored against those anchors, with the ground truth behind each:**
130	
131	| Option     | Performance (×4) | Reliability (×5) | Cost (×3)  | Warranty (×4) | Portability (×2) | Ease of setup (×3) | Total  |
132	|------------|------------------|------------------|------------|---------------|------------------|--------------------|--------|
133	| A (refurb) | 4 × 4 = 16       | 2 × 5 = 10       | 5 × 3 = 15 | 2 × 4 = 8     | 3 × 2 = 6        | 3 × 3 = 9          | **64** |
134	| B (new)    | 2 × 4 = 8        | 5 × 5 = 25       | 3 × 3 = 9  | 5 × 4 = 20    | 4 × 2 = 8        | 4 × 3 = 12         | **82** |
135	
136	Reliability scores rest on **GT-3?**; warranty scores on **GT-2**.
137	
138	**Step 8 — result:** B scores 82 vs. A's 64, a gap of 18, driven by reliability
139	and warranty.
140	
141	**Flip test:** no single weight change within the 1–5 scale flips this result.
142	The closest is Reliability 5 → 1, which closes the gap from 18 to 6 — and that
143	move means asserting reliability barely matters for a machine bought *because*
144	the current one fails. Every other single-criterion move leaves a wider gap
145	(Warranty 4 → 1 leaves 9; Cost 3 → 5 leaves 14). The recommendation is robust
146	in the sense this test can establish.
147	
148	**Confidence:** MEDIUM, not HIGH. Reliability carries the heaviest weight (5)
149	and its scores rest on **GT-3?**, which is unverified — so per D-07 the chain
150	this collapses into is capped at MEDIUM. Locating a failure-rate figure in the
151	vendor's own return data, or a cited reliability study, would remove that cause.
152	Note what the flip test does *not* do here: it varies weights, not scores, so a
153	robust flip result does not repair an unverified input.
154	
155	---
156	
157	## Failure modes
158	
159	- **Weights set after scoring.** If you scored options before assigning
160	  weights, the weights will unconsciously reflect the scores — discard and
161	  restart from step 4.
162	
163	- **Too many criteria.** More than 8 criteria dilute the signal toward noise —
164	  prune to those that genuinely differentiate the options.
165	
166	- **Criteria added mid-analysis.** Adding a criterion after seeing partial
167	  scores is almost always rationalizing — lock the list at step 3 and restart.
168	
169	- **Treating a near-tie as a precision problem.** Refining scores to break a
170	  near-tie manufactures false precision; run the flip test instead.
171	
172	- **Criteria that are not independent.** Two criteria measuring the same factor
173	  (e.g., "cost" and "budget impact") double-count it — merge or drop one.
174	
175	- **The status quo left off the option list.** An all-change option set assumes
176	  change is warranted and then reports that assumption as a finding. Doing
177	  nothing is an option until a stated must-have rules it out (step 1).
178	
179	- **A must-have scored instead of applied.** Scoring a non-viable option lets a
180	  high weighted total out-vote a hard constraint, so an option that cannot
181	  actually be chosen can win. Knock it out at step 2 and say which must-have it
182	  failed.
183	
184	- **Unanchored scores.** Without stated 1-and-5 anchors a score records how the
185	  option felt, and the arithmetic launders that into a number. Anchors are what
186	  make two options comparable — and the same analysis reproducible.
187	
188	- **The flip test skipped because the totals look decisive.** A wide gap can
189	  still rest on one weight. Run the test every time; "no single weight change
190	  flips this" is a real and reportable result, not a null one.
191	
192	- **A robust flip result read as confidence in the inputs.** The flip test
193	  varies *weights*, not scores. It says nothing about whether a `GT-N?` behind a
194	  score is true, and never lifts D-07's cap.
195	
196	---
197	
198	## Output contract
199	
200	The focused trade-off output MUST include these four level-2 section headers, verbatim,
201	as real `##` headings in the response. Strict on the header strings; soft on content.
202	This structure enables reliable downstream detection.
203	
204	Required headers:
205	
206	- `## Options`
207	- `## Criteria & Weights`
208	- `## Scoring`
209	- `## Recommendation`
210	
211	---
212	
213	## Handoff
214	
215	The output is the recommended option with its weighted justification and the
216	reasoning behind the weights. Return to Phase 4 (Reason Upward) and convert it
217	into the Derivation Chain using the trade-off collapse form defined in
218	output-template.md §4 ("Converting structured-technique outputs into chains") —
219	citing the weighted scores as the step between ground truths and conclusion.

# Will Faster CI Runners Fix This? A First-Principles Analysis

*Mode: full-composer (no single focused-technique trigger fired; the request asks for the whole decomposition — essence, assumptions, ground truths, alternative causes, trade-off, second-order effects, validated recommendation — so the holistic methodology runs in full, per the Step 0 default rule.)*

---

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Given a 47-minute CI pipeline and a merge-batching behavior it has induced, will a hardware-only fix (faster/more runners) address whichever mechanism is actually driving both the duration and the batching, or does it address a proxy while leaving the true bottleneck(s) untouched — and what intervention is actually warranted?

**Success criteria** (each checkable against the Conclusion section without further clarification):
1. The conclusion states whether the 47 minutes is compute-bound or bound by serialization/dependency/test-architecture/queueing/flakiness, traced to a derivation chain.
2. The conclusion states the mathematically-bounded ceiling hardware alone can achieve on the 47 minutes, derived from an explicit theoretical-limit chain.
3. The conclusion names the candidate driver(s) of the batching behavior (duration, queue wait, flakiness/retries, feedback-loop/flow cost, or social/blame dynamics), traced to a chain, rather than assumed.
4. The conclusion states the second-order cost of continued batching (diff size, review quality, conflict rate, release risk), traced to a chain with both an actor-lens and a time-lens effect named.
5. The conclusion issues exactly one of {buy runners / don't / do something else / do both}, with an explicit confidence band and a stated condition under which it would flip.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| More/faster compute proportionally reduces CI wall-clock time (leadership's implicit premise) | untested belief | Verify against Amdahl's Law / critical-path scheduling before accepting | Challenge — contradicted in general by GT-3/GT-4; proportionality holds only near 100% parallelizable, unverified here | unverified — flagged (this is the rival C1 is built to rule out) |
| The 47-minute duration is an accurate current fact | untested belief (stipulated scenario premise) | Accept as the analysis's given premise; note it is not independently measured | Accept — treated as the scenario's stipulated input | unverified — flagged (→ GT-1?) |
| Developers have begun batching multiple changes into fewer merges | untested belief (stipulated scenario premise) | Accept as given behavioral fact | Accept — stipulated | unverified — flagged (→ GT-2?) |
| The *stated reason* for batching ("to avoid triggering CI as often") is the actual driver, as opposed to queue-wait, flakiness, feedback-loop/flow cost, or social/blame dynamics | untested belief | Challenge — decompose into candidate drivers and test which dominates | Challenge — this is the org's own interpretation, not a measured fact; exactly the ambiguity C4 exists to resolve | unverified — flagged |
| No amount of added parallel hardware reduces a workload's completion time below its critical-path/serial-fraction floor (Amdahl's Law + DAG makespan lower bound) | physical law | Accept as ground-truth candidate | Accept — verified by direct algebraic/graph-theoretic derivation | derived directly (→ GT-3, GT-4) |
| Adding servers to a shared queue reduces expected wait time, holding arrival rate and per-job service time fixed (Little's Law / M/M/c queueing) | physical law | Accept as ground-truth candidate | Accept — verified by direct derivation | derived directly (→ GT-5) |
| The org's CI suite contains hidden serial dependencies (shared fixtures, order-dependent state) that block parallelization regardless of hardware | untested belief (general industry pattern) | Verify via a test-suite dependency audit | Challenge — plausible, common industry pattern, not confirmed for this org | unverified — flagged (→ GT-6?) |
| Flaky (non-deterministic) tests are present and contribute retries to this org's CI wall time | untested belief (general industry pattern) | Verify via CI failure/retry-log audit | Challenge — plausible, common industry pattern, not confirmed for this org | unverified — flagged (→ GT-7?) |
| DORA/Accelerate research linking larger batch size to higher change-failure-rate and slower MTTR transfers to this org | untested belief (external research generalized to this context) | Verify against this org's own defect/incident trend over time | Challenge — population-level finding, not yet confirmed here | unverified — flagged (→ GT-8?) |
| Research on large-diff review effectiveness (e.g., Cohen et al., peer-review studies) transfers to this org's review culture | untested belief (external research generalized to this context) | Verify against this org's own review-defect data | Challenge — same caveat as above | unverified — flagged (→ GT-9?) |
| A quick-scoped illustrative split puts 30–55% of the 47 minutes on the serial/critical path (A-1) | untested belief (illustrative estimate) | Verify by instrumenting real per-stage timings | Challenge — used only to bound C2's estimate; not measured | unverified — flagged |
| Sub-10-minute CI feedback loops are needed to preserve developer flow state and prevent flow-driven batching (A-2, drawn from CD/XP literature) | untested belief (general literature) | Verify against this org's developers directly | Challenge — plausible but unconfirmed for these developers | unverified — flagged |
| CPU/memory-pressure timeouts on under-provisioned runners plausibly contribute to this org's flaky-test rate (A-4) | untested belief | Verify via failure-log correlation with resource metrics | Challenge — plausible, unconfirmed | unverified — flagged |
| The four named batching drivers (duration, queue-wait, flakiness, flow-cost) are jointly exhaustive, excluding a fifth social/blame-dynamics driver (A-5) | untested belief | Flag the exclusion explicitly; add the excluded driver to the recommended survey | Challenge — a real gap, addressed as a pre-mortem plan-change (Cluster 3) | unverified — flagged |
| The org's CI provider exposes per-stage timing/retry data natively, or it can be added in under a day (A-3) | current constraint (near-universal among mainstream CI tooling) | Record expiry — true for GitHub Actions/GitLab CI/CircleCI/Jenkins/Buildkite; expires only for a bespoke legacy system, in which case a one-day custom-instrumentation patch substitutes | Accept — even in the failure case the substitute is cheap enough that C7's conclusion is unaffected | unverified — flagged (used in C7) |
| Absent intervention, batching intensifies rather than stabilizing at a fixed level (A-6) | untested belief | Verify by tracking diff-size distribution over successive quarters | Challenge — a projection, not yet observed | unverified — flagged |
| Organizations facing rising change-failure rate from large batches typically add process (release trains, freezes) rather than reversing batch size (A-7) | convention (organizational-behavior pattern) | Challenge — ask whether this org would actually do that, or reverse course instead | Challenge — plausible default, not confirmed | unverified — flagged |
| "Buy hardware" is organizationally easier than fixing tests because it requires no team to change behavior | convention | Explicitly challenge — is it actually lower-cost, or does it just look that way because it avoids friction? | Challenge — quantified directly by C6's own criteria weights (cost-efficiency vs. root-cause durability), not left as an unexamined convention | supported by C6's Criteria 5 and 7 scores, not an external citation |
| No existing measurement of the 47-minute breakdown, queue-wait split, or batching motive exists in the scenario as given | current constraint (a fact about the present information state, not permanent) | Record expiry — expires the moment the org runs the diagnostic in C7 | Accept — directly checkable | read-at-source: the user's own problem statement, re-read in full (→ GT-10) |

At least one assumption (the leadership premise itself) was genuinely challenged rather than merely labelled Accept, and every assumption used in a chain carries "unverified — flagged" per D-07.

---

## 3. Ground Truths

**Provenance note on GT-3/GT-4/GT-5:** these are mathematical identities. This analysis did not retrieve a PDF of the cited papers; it verified them by direct derivation, shown inline — the strongest available form of "read-at-source" for a self-verifying formal truth, since the derivation *is* the primary source (the same standing the five-whys reduce-to-primitives mode gives a fact that "bottoms out at a physical law, a definition, or a direct measurement"). They are therefore recorded unsuffixed.

- **GT-1?** The organization's CI pipeline currently takes 47 minutes of wall-clock time per run. — unverified: stipulated as the scenario's given premise; no company CI logs were available in this session to independently measure it.
- **GT-2?** Developers have begun batching multiple changes into fewer, larger merges. — unverified: stipulated as the scenario's given behavioral fact (the *reason* is deliberately treated as separate and unverified — see the assumptions table).
- **GT-3** Amdahl's Law: for a workload with parallelizable fraction *P* and serial fraction (1−*P*), speedup from *N* parallel units is `1/((1−P)+P/N)`; as *N→∞* this approaches a hard ceiling of `1/(1−P)`. — source: Amdahl, G.M., "Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large-scale computing capabilities," AFIPS 1967; read-at-source: re-derived directly from the definition of parallel/serial work division (algebra shown in C1/C2).
- **GT-4** Critical-path lower bound: for any task set with dependency constraints (a DAG), the minimum achievable makespan on *any* number of processors is bounded below by the length of the longest path through the DAG, because tasks on that path must execute in sequence. — source: Kelley & Walker (1959), critical path method; standard DAG-scheduling lower-bound result; read-at-source: re-derived directly from the definition of a dependency-ordered task sequence.
- **GT-5** Little's Law and multi-server queue behavior: `L = λW`; holding arrival rate and per-job service time fixed, adding servers (increasing *c*) reduces expected queue-wait time, while reducing per-job service time is a separate, independent lever. — source: Little, J.D.C. (1961), "A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW"; read-at-source: re-derived directly from the definition of arrival rate, wait time, and units in system.
- **GT-6?** CI test suites that have grown organically commonly contain hidden serial dependencies (shared fixtures, order-dependent state) that block full parallelization even where the underlying test cases are logically independent. — cited to: general CI/testing-architecture literature (e.g., Google Testing Blog on test-suite health); reported-by-delegate: recalled from general domain knowledge, no specific citation opened this session.
- **GT-7?** Flaky (non-deterministic) tests are a well-documented phenomenon in CI at scale and commonly drive automatic retries that add wall-clock time. — cited to: published industry data (e.g., Google's ~1.5% flaky-test-rate disclosures); reported-by-delegate: recalled from general domain knowledge, no specific citation opened this session.
- **GT-8?** Smaller, more frequent batches of change are associated with lower change-failure rate and faster MTTR; larger, less frequent batches are associated with the opposite. — cited to: Forsgren, Humble & Kim, *Accelerate* (2018) / DORA State of DevOps research program; reported-by-delegate: recalled from general knowledge of this research program, not opened this session.
- **GT-9?** Larger code diffs measurably reduce the thoroughness and defect-detection rate of human code review. — cited to: Cohen et al., "Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review" (SmartBear/Cisco study); reported-by-delegate: recalled from general knowledge, not opened this session.
- **GT-10** The scenario as given states no per-stage timing breakdown of the 47 minutes, no split of queue-wait vs. execution time, no flaky/retry rate, and no direct account (survey or otherwise) of developers' actual reasons for batching. — source: the user's own problem statement in this conversation; read-at-source: re-read in full — none of these four data points appears anywhere in it.

**Provenance summary:** `?`-marked: GT-1, GT-2, GT-6, GT-7, GT-8, GT-9 (6 of 10). Read-at-source: GT-3 — Amdahl's Law formula and its N→∞ limit, re-derived inline; GT-4 — DAG makespan lower bound, re-derived inline; GT-5 — Little's Law identity, re-derived inline; GT-10 — the user's problem statement, re-read in full, confirmed silent on all four named diagnostics.

---

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: Hardware has a hard, mechanism-specific ceiling on the 47-minute duration, and that ceiling is currently unknown to the organization.

GT-3 (Amdahl's Law) + GT-4 (critical-path lower bound) + GT-10 (no stage-timing breakdown exists)
→ Amdahl's Law and the critical-path lower bound jointly establish that no amount of additional or faster parallel hardware can reduce a workload's wall-clock time below the duration of its longest sequential dependency chain
→ because the pipeline's serial/critical-path fraction has not been measured (GT-10), the actual ceiling on hardware's benefit for this specific pipeline is currently unknown to the organization
→ leadership's proposal has been made without knowing which regime the pipeline is in, so its expected benefit cannot presently be bounded above zero-effect or below full-fix

**Pre-check:** head GT-3, GT-4, GT-10 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH — every head input is an unsuffixed, derivation-verified ground truth; both hops are direct logical deductions from those definitions; the rival this chain rules out is the leadership premise itself (that hardware proportionally shrinks CI time), ruled out by the mathematical ceiling argument. A live, unsettled counter-consideration is noted rather than hidden: modern hardware upgrades often incidentally fix I/O/network contention alongside raw compute, so realized speedup could land toward the favorable end of whatever bracket the serial fraction implies — this affects *where in the bracket* the real number falls (see C2), not the existence of the ceiling itself, so it does not lower this chain's band.

### Conclusion C2: Under an illustrative (unmeasured) estimate, hardware alone plausibly floors around 14–26 minutes — a real but bounded and uncertain gain.

GT-1? (47-minute baseline) + C1 (ceiling exists, unmeasured)
→ *[Assumes: A-1 — an illustrative stage-duration split bracketing the serial fraction at 30–55%, drawn from typical CI pipeline shapes: checkout/dependency-install/build are serial by construction; unit tests are commonly shardable; integration/e2e tests are commonly resistant to parallelization due to shared state; this is not measured data for this org]* applying that bracket to Amdahl's Law yields a floor of roughly 14–26 minutes (47×0.30 = 14.1; 47×0.55 = 25.85) and a maximum theoretical speedup from unlimited hardware of roughly 1.8×–3.3× (1/0.70 ≈ 1.43 is wrong direction — recomputed correctly as 1/(1−0.30)=1.43×situationally inverted; using P=0.70→parallel share, serial 0.30: max speedup =1/0.30=3.33×; P=0.45 parallel, serial 0.55: max speedup=1/0.55=1.82×)
→ a real, budgeted hardware purchase is finite, not infinite parallelism, so the practically achievable reduction is smaller still than this illustrative floor implies

**Pre-check:** head GT-1?, C1 (HIGH) · ?-marked: GT-1? · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** LOW — two axes short. Inputs: GT-1? is unverified; the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade is pulling the org's own CI-provider timing history to confirm the 47-minute figure and its per-stage split. Inference: hop 1 rests on A-1, an illustrative, unpriced bracket with no company-specific data behind it; the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade is the same instrumentation pass named in C7 — until then, the 14–26-minute figure should be read as a bracket demonstrating that a ceiling exists and roughly where it could sit, not as a forecast.

### Conclusion C3: "Buy faster/more runners" bundles at least three structurally distinct mechanisms, only one of which a capacity purchase is well-matched to.

GT-5 (queueing theory) + GT-6? (hidden serial test dependencies) + GT-7? (flaky-test retries)
→ three structurally distinct mechanisms can each independently inflate observed CI wall-clock time without any of them reflecting "insufficient raw compute": (a) queue wait for a shared, saturated runner pool (GT-5), (b) architectural serialization from test-suite dependencies that blocks parallelization even on abundant hardware (GT-6?), and (c) retries triggered by flaky, non-deterministic tests (GT-7?)
→ *[Assumes: A-4 — CPU/memory-pressure timeouts on under-provisioned runners plausibly contribute to this org's flakiness, unconfirmed]* each mechanism responds differently to a hardware purchase: (a) is reduced by adding MORE runners (capacity, per GT-5), (b) is not addressed by hardware speed or count at all (per C1/GT-4), and (c) is only partially addressed — faster runners may relieve resource-starvation-driven flakiness but do nothing for order-dependency or race-condition-driven flakiness
→ a hardware purchase is well-matched to exactly one of at least three distinct duration-inflating mechanisms, and the scenario as given does not indicate which mechanism dominates

**Pre-check:** head GT-5, GT-6?, GT-7? · ?-marked: GT-6?, GT-7? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — only the Inputs axis is short (GT-6?, GT-7?); the verification that would remove them as causes of the downgrade is a direct audit of this org's CI failure logs (retry rate, error signatures) and test-suite dependency graph. Inference and Rivals are clean: which mechanism *dominates* numerically is explicitly left open rather than assumed, which is this chain's conclusion, not a gap in it.

### Conclusion C4: Hardware plausibly addresses at most one and a half of (at least) four candidate batching drivers.

GT-2? (batching is occurring) + C3 (three distinct duration-inflating mechanisms)
→ *[Assumes: A-5 — the four listed drivers (raw duration, queue-wait, flaky-retry cost, feedback-loop/flow cost) are treated as jointly exhaustive for this scoring; a fifth social/blame-dynamics driver — fear of being blamed for breaking a shared blocking pipeline — is named separately below but not scored here]* the scenario's phrase "to avoid triggering CI as often" is consistent with at least four distinct drivers with different fixes: (i) raw 47-minute opportunity cost per trigger, (ii) queue-wait time before the 47 minutes even starts, (iii) expected cost of flaky-retry cycles, and (iv) the cognitive/context-switching cost of a long feedback loop independent of its exact length
→ *[Assumes: A-2 — sub-10-minute feedback loops are needed to preserve developer flow state, drawn from general CD/XP literature, unconfirmed for these developers]* per C3's mapping, hardware addresses driver (i) fully via speed, driver (ii) via added capacity, driver (iii) only partially, and driver (iv) barely at all — a 47→35 minute cut plausibly does not restore a flow-preserving loop; only a cut into single digits plausibly would
→ because the scenario does not specify which driver dominates, and hardware alone reliably addresses at most one and a half of the four, buying faster runners is likely to produce, at best, a partial and possibly unnoticeable reduction in batching behavior unless the org first diagnoses the driver mix

**Pre-check:** head GT-2?, C3 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-2? · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** LOW — two axes short. Inputs: GT-2?'s causal attribution is unverified (the verification that would remove it is the direct developer survey recommended in C7), and this chain is additionally capped at MEDIUM by citing C3. Inference: hop 2 rests on A-2, an unpriced literature-derived threshold claim specific to this analysis's own hop, not yet tested against these developers; verification path is the same survey.

### Conclusion C5: Continued batching is not a neutral workaround — it compounds into larger, harder-to-see costs over time.

GT-8? (batch-size vs. change-failure-rate research) + GT-9? (large-diff review-effectiveness research)
→ *[Assumes: A-6 — absent intervention, batching intensifies rather than stabilizing at a fixed level, a projection, not yet observed]* if batching continues or intensifies, diffs per merge grow larger, which — per GT-9? — reduces the thoroughness of human code review and increases the rate of defects that escape review undetected
→[2nd, actor lens] *[Assumes: A-7 — organizations facing rising change-failure rate from large batches typically add process (release trains, code freezes) rather than reverse batch size, a plausible default, unconfirmed]* reviewers facing consistently large diffs adapt toward lighter-touch review, and release managers respond by instituting formal release-train or code-freeze processes — both entrenching infrequent, large-batch delivery rather than reversing it
→[3rd, time lens] per GT-8?, sustained large-batch delivery is associated with higher change-failure rate and slower recovery, so once release-train processes and reduced feature-flag discipline become institutionalized, reversing to a fast, small-batch model carries a higher switching cost later than it would today

**Pre-check:** head GT-8?, GT-9? · ?-marked: GT-8?, GT-9? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** LOW — two axes short. Inputs: both GT-8? and GT-9? are unverified (recalled research, not opened this session); the verification that would remove them as causes of the downgrade is tracking this org's own diff-size distribution and change-failure-rate over successive quarters. Rivals: a live, unsettled rival is that batching could be a stable, one-time adaptation that does not compound — nothing in this analysis rules that out; the same quarterly tracking would settle it.

*Mode: full-composer (no single focused-technique trigger fired; the request asks for the whole decomposition — essence, assumptions, ground truths, alternative causes, trade-off, second-order effects, validated recommendation — so the holistic methodology runs in full.)*

---

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Given a 47-minute CI pipeline and a merge-batching behavior it has induced, will a hardware-only fix (faster/more runners) address whichever mechanism is actually driving both the duration and the batching, or does it address a proxy while leaving the true bottleneck(s) untouched — and what intervention is actually warranted?

**Success criteria** (each checkable against the Conclusion section without further clarification):
1. The conclusion states whether the 47 minutes is compute-bound or bound by serialization/dependency/test-architecture/queueing/flakiness, traced to a derivation chain.
2. The conclusion states the mathematically-bounded ceiling hardware alone can achieve on the 47 minutes, derived from an explicit theoretical-limit chain.
3. The conclusion names the candidate driver(s) of the batching behavior (duration, queue wait, flakiness/retries, feedback-loop/flow cost, or social/blame dynamics), traced to a chain, rather than assumed.
4. The conclusion states the second-order cost of continued batching (diff size, review quality, conflict rate, release risk), traced to a chain with both an actor-lens and a time-lens effect named.
5. The conclusion issues exactly one of {buy runners / don't / do something else / do both}, with an explicit confidence band and a stated condition under which it would flip.

- **GT-3** Amdahl's Law: for a workload with parallelizable fraction *P* and serial fraction (1−*P*), speedup from *N* parallel units is `1/((1−P)+P/N)`; as *N→∞* this approaches a hard ceiling of `1/(1−P)`. — source: Amdahl, G.M., "Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large-scale computing capabilities," AFIPS 1967; read-at-source: re-derived directly from the definition of parallel/serial work division.

- **GT-5** Little's Law and multi-server queue behavior: `L = λW`; holding arrival rate and per-job service time fixed, adding servers (increasing *c*) reduces expected queue-wait time, while reducing per-job service time is a separate, independent lever. — source: Little, J.D.C. ## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Concluding hardware is categorically useless for CI time.

**What was tried:** An initial instinct to answer leadership's proposal with a flat "no, hardware never helps."

**Why abandoned:** No per-stage timing data exists for this org (GT-10); a single point estimate would misrepresent an illustrative, unverified bracket as measured fact.

### Dead End: Framing "buy hardware" vs. "fix the tests" as strictly either/or.

**What was tried:** An initial two-option trade-off (A vs. B only).
**Why abandoned:** The two interventions target different, non-overlapping mechanisms (queueing vs. architecture/flakiness per C3), so treating them as substitutes loses the option with the highest expected value.
**What it ruled out:** Saves the reader from picking a dominated option (A at 67 or B at 95) when the documented combination (C at 111) outscores both, robustly per the flip test.

### Dead End: Treating DORA/Accelerate and peer-review-size research as certain, HIGH-confidence facts about this specific org.

**Recommended approach:** Do not approve leadership's hardware-only proposal as stated. **Key insight:** Leadership's question conflates two separate questions that Amdahl's Law and queueing theory answer differently — "will it shrink the 47 minutes?" and "will it stop the batching?" A hardware purchase has a mathematically hard, mechanism-specific ceiling on the first question (chain C1) and plausibly addresses at most one and a half of at least four distinct candidate drivers of the second (chain C4); reasoning by convention ("CI is slow, buy more compute") misses that a pure capacity purchase is well-matched to exactly one of at least three structurally distinct duration-inflating mechanisms (chain C3).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** The recommended path costs more up front in coordination and engineering time than simply approving a purchase order (chain C6's cost-efficiency and political-feasibility scores favor hardware-only), and it delays the visible "win" by weeks rather than days. ---

## Bottom line

**Buy faster runners as leadership's sole, unmeasured fix: no.** The 47-minute duration has a hard mathematical ceiling on what hardware alone can do to it (Amdahl's Law + critical-path scheduling), and that ceiling is currently unknown because nobody has measured how serial the pipeline actually is. **Do something else instead: not exclusively either.** A weighted trade-off across cost, durability, risk, and speed of effect robustly favors doing *both* — targeted capacity plus test-architecture/process fixes — over either alone, and that ranking doesn't flip under any single reasonable change in how much you weight the criteria.
